input.command: cat -n src/ci.ts; ls; ls src; grep -rn "getBuild\|fetch\|timeout\|AbortSignal" src --include=*.ts | head -50
cat -n src/routes.ts; cat package.json; grep -rn "setGlobalDispatcher\|headersTimeout\|bodyTimeout\|race" src

input.reason: In src/ci.ts:4, `getBuild` calls `fetch(`${CI}/builds/${id}`)` with no options: no `signal`, no `AbortSignal.timeout`, and nothing wraps it in a timeout. The only caller is the `build` route handler in src/routes.ts:52, which awaits `getBuild` directly and has no timeout, race, or abort of its own. I searched src for a global dispatcher or timeout setting (setGlobalDispatcher, headersTimeout, bodyTimeout, race) and found none. package.json has no dependencies that add one. When the CI server accepts the connection but is slow to answer, each build request stays pending. The only limit is Node's built-in undici default: about 300 s for headers and about 300 s between body chunks. The claim overstates one point. Requests do not hang forever, and one stalled call does not block other callers. Each call that hits a stalled CI waits separately for up to several minutes. The missing request timeout is still a real reliability defect.
input.failure_scenario: ci.example.com accepts TCP connections but stops responding, for example because it is overloaded or a proxy is holding requests. Every call to the `build` route (src/routes.ts:52) awaits `getBuild` and stays pending until undici's default headers timeout of about 5 minutes fires. Until then, each request holds a socket and memory. Clients get no response and no quick error, and pending requests pile up during the outage.
input.severity_reason: This only happens when the CI dependency is degraded. Node's fetch also has built-in timeouts of about 300 s, so requests end eventually rather than hanging forever, and one stalled call does not block other callers. It is a real reliability risk on one route, not an outage on a common path.
